analyses.title: Beyond Precision: Importance-Aware Recall for Factuality Evaluation in Long-Form LLM Generation
analyses.research_question: How can long-form LLM factuality evaluation measure not only whether generated claims are evidence-supported but also whether the response omits relevant and important facts?
analyses.methodology: The paper constructs retrieval-conditioned reference fact sets from external knowledge sources, decomposes retrieved passages into atomic facts, deduplicates them, and scores each fact for query relevance and topic salience. Generated responses are separately decomposed into atomic claims; LLM judges then assess claim support for factual precision and reference-fact coverage for factual recall, including an importance-weighted recall variant and an F1 combination. The framework is evaluated with six LLMs across FactScore biography prompts, a stratified sample of LongFact, and a sample of LongForm prompts.

key_findings.finding: Fine-grained recall exposes factual incompleteness that precision-only evaluation cannot measure, because reference facts absent from the generation are scored explicitly.

The evaluated models show severe recall limitations in the biography and LongForm settings, while LongFact exhibits different precision-recall operating points and several models attain recall comparable to or above precision.
Longer generation is neither necessary nor sufficient for better factuality; excessive claim production can raise recall while lowering precision.
key_findings.section: 4.2.1 Claim to fact ratio and the precision–recall trade-off

key_findings.finding: Unsupported claims are reported as more common than directly contradicted claims across the evaluated models and datasets, while biography generation has comparatively elevated contradiction rates.
For very small reference-fact budgets, salience is especially useful for identifying facts models tend to cover first, whereas relevance becomes more important as broader fact coverage is considered.

The text states that GPT-4o-mini has a 44.4% LongFact F1, but Table 1 reports 36.8 F1 for GPT-4o-mini and assigns 44.4 to Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite recall, so that exact numerical statement is inconsistent with the table.

limitations: Recall quality depends on the completeness, correctness, and consistency of the retrieved external evidence used to construct the reference fact set.
Errors can propagate through retrieval, reference-fact extraction, claim decomposition, importance scoring, coverage judgment, and claim verification.
The empirical evaluation is restricted to the selected models, datasets, and domains.
The framework evaluates a reference fact inventory induced by retrieved evidence, so facts absent from retrieval cannot contribute to measured recall.
The study does not directly evaluate temporal validity, version-aware provenance, calibrated abstention, or robustness under explicit non-stationary distribution shift.
raw_claims: The framework evaluates factual precision and factual recall as complementary properties of long-form generation.
Reference facts are extracted from query-conditioned external evidence rather than inferred only from model outputs.
Facts receive importance scores combining query relevance and topic salience.
Factual recall measures how many reference facts are covered by the generated response.
Importance-weighted recall gives greater weight to covered facts judged more relevant or salient.
Factual precision counts the fraction of generated atomic claims supported by retrieved evidence.
The experiments use FactScore biographies, LongFact, and LongForm prompts.
Different models occupy different precision-recall operating points across domains.
Producing more claims can improve recall without producing better overall factuality.
Most factual errors observed by the authors are classified as unsupported rather than direct contradictions.
Biography generation exhibits relatively high direct-contradiction rates.
Salience is particularly useful when evaluation focuses only on the single most important fact.
The quality of recall estimates is bounded by the quality of retrieved evidence.

analyses.title: Evaluating Attribution in Dialogue Systems: The BEGIN Benchmark
analyses.research_question: How reliably do existing automatic metrics identify whether knowledge-grounded dialogue responses are actually attributable to the supplied evidence, including under challenging forms of distribution shift?
analyses.methodology: The authors build BEGIN from roughly 12,000 dialogue turns produced by neural dialogue systems trained on three knowledge-grounded dialogue corpora and obtain human labels using a three-way taxonomy of attributable, unattributable, and generic responses. They meta-evaluate eight families of automatic attribution metrics, including lexical-overlap, semantic-similarity, QA-based, and NLI-based approaches, and create an 8,000-example adversarially augmented silver training set for attribution classifiers. Robustness analyses stratify examples by extractivity and compare performance across corpora with substantially different knowledge-source lengths.

key_findings.finding: Existing automatic metrics do not reliably separate attributable abstractive responses from unattributable responses.
key_findings.section: 4.4 Are Metrics Measuring Attribution or Extractivity?

key_findings.finding: All evaluated metric families exhibit a strong dependence on lexical overlap or extractivity rather than a robust semantic understanding of attribution.
key_findings.section: 4.4 Are Metrics Measuring Attribution or Extractivity?

key_findings.finding: Unattributable but highly extractive responses can receive higher scores than attributable responses expressed through abstraction or paraphrase.
key_findings.section: 4.4 Are Metrics Measuring Attribution or Extractivity?

key_findings.finding: Metrics perform substantially worse when the grounding knowledge source is longer, demonstrating a concrete distribution-shift and robustness failure.

Training on the paper's adversarial attribution data provides stronger supervision than the tested NLI-style datasets for the BEGIN taxonomy, but classifier performance remains far below human annotation quality.
None of the tested classifier configurations exceeds 46% macro F1 on the benchmark, while human annotations compared with majority vote exceed 95% precision.

limitations: BEGIN covers three knowledge-grounded dialogue corpora and therefore does not establish robustness across all dialogue domains or other free-form generation tasks.
Its three-way taxonomy tests attribution to provided knowledge but does not directly measure whether important source information was omitted from a response.
The examined distribution shifts emphasize extractivity and knowledge-source length rather than temporal drift, changing document versions, or source recency.
Generic responses are modeled as a distinct category, but the benchmark does not provide calibrated risk or utility thresholds for deciding when a system should abstain.
The benchmark focuses on grounding against a supplied knowledge source and does not integrate multi-source temporal provenance.
raw_claims: BEGIN contains about twelve thousand generated knowledge-grounded dialogue turns.
Responses are human-labeled as attributable, unattributable, or generic.
The benchmark draws from three knowledge-grounded dialogue datasets.
The study evaluates eight automatic attribution metrics.
A separate adversarially generated training set contains about eight thousand examples.
Current metrics systematically benefit responses that copy wording from their evidence.
Attributable paraphrases are harder for existing metrics to recognize than highly extractive responses.
High lexical overlap can cause unattributable responses to be scored as attributable.
Metric performance declines as grounding documents become longer.
The benchmark therefore exposes robustness failures that ordinary aggregate correlation can hide.
NLI-oriented training does not fully capture the broader category of unverifiable information.
The authors argue that acknowledgment of ignorance should not be treated like a misleading unsupported assertion.
Current classifier metrics remain substantially below human attribution judgments.
BEGIN is publicly released as a benchmark resource.

analyses.title: Merging Facts, Crafting Fallacies: Evaluating the Contradictory Nature of Aggregated Factual Claims in Long-Form Generations
analyses.research_question: Can a long-form response be globally misleading even when its individual atomic claims are independently verifiable, and how should factuality metrics detect this failure under entity ambiguity?
analyses.methodology: The authors construct AmbigBio by randomly selecting 500 ambiguous names from Wikipedia disambiguation pages and use RAG to generate biographies from top-five retrieved Wikipedia passages. They demonstrate that models can combine true statements about different same-named entities into a single misleading biography, then extend FActScore into D-FActScore by grouping claims according to the entity a reader would perceive them as describing, linking each group to one entity, and verifying all facts in that group against that entity's evidence. Human annotation on generated biographies is compared with an automatic GPT-3.5/ChatGPT-based evaluation pipeline, followed by experiments across multiple LLMs and prompting conditions.

key_findings.finding: Independent verification of atomic claims can substantially overestimate paragraph-level factuality when true facts about multiple entities are merged into a narrative that appears to describe one entity.
Human D-FActScore is 8 to 16 percentage points lower than FActScore for the tested Llama and Tulu generations, exposing entity-mixing errors hidden by independent claim verification.
FActScore and D-FActScore can reverse the relative ordering of systems because copying individually supportable sentences does not guarantee correct entity-level aggregation.
The automatic D-FActScore pipeline reproduces the same model ordering as human evaluation and has an overall per-paragraph Pearson correlation of 0.75 with human D-FActScore.
Providing demonstrations containing ambiguous names does not improve D-FActScore relative to demonstrations without ambiguity in the reported experiments.
Increasing Llama model size from 13B to 70B yields less than a two-point D-FActScore improvement, indicating that scaling alone does not resolve the tested entity-disambiguation failure.

limitations: The empirical study is centered on human-biography generation rather than diverse long-form generation domains.
Both retrieval and fact verification use Wikipedia, so results do not establish performance with heterogeneous or unstructured multi-source evidence.
D-FActScore assumes that evidence can be partitioned or linked to distinct entities; applying it to ambiguous unstructured Web evidence may require substantially harder entity resolution.
The automatic evaluator depends on GPT-3.5/ChatGPT for decomposition, grouping, and fact verification and systematically yields somewhat higher D-FActScore than human annotation.
The work studies entity ambiguity but not temporal inconsistency, conflicting source versions, calibrated abstention, or general non-stationary distribution shift.
raw_claims: A paragraph can be misleading even when every atomic statement can be supported somewhere in the knowledge source.
AmbigBio contains 500 ambiguous names sampled from Wikipedia disambiguation pages.
Each AmbigBio name corresponds on average to multiple distinct Wikipedia entities.
The generation experiments retrieve five Wikipedia passages for each target name.
FActScore verifies atomic claims independently and can therefore miss cross-claim entity inconsistency.
D-FActScore groups facts that the paragraph presents as belonging to the same distinguishable entity.
Each D-FActScore fact group is linked to one entity before its claims are verified.
Human evaluation shows substantial gaps between FActScore and D-FActScore for models that mix entities.
FActScore and D-FActScore produce different relative system rankings in the reported comparison.
The automatic D-FActScore pipeline uses language models for fact extraction, grouping, entity linking, and verification.
Automatic and human D-FActScore produce the same ordering of the three models in the validation experiment.
Automatic D-FActScore is somewhat more optimistic than human D-FActScore.
Ambiguous-name demonstrations do not eliminate entity-mixing errors.
The paper releases AmbigBio and D-FActScore code.

analyses.title: Towards Query-Agnostic RAG Evaluation via Query Coverage and Claim Verifiability
analyses.research_question: Can a reference-free RAG evaluation framework provide consistent fine-grained retrieval and generation diagnostics for both close-ended and open-ended queries by combining query coverage with claim verifiability?
analyses.methodology: Q-CARE decomposes each query into atomic sub-queries and each generated answer into atomic claims, then performs alignment checks between sub-queries, retrieved chunks, and answer claims. These alignments define coverage-aware retrieval metrics C-Prec@k and C-nDCG@k and generator metrics for Completeness, Conciseness, and Verifiableness without requiring gold answers or gold evidence chunks. The authors construct a human-annotated evaluation set spanning eight datasets, sample 160 close-ended and 160 open-ended queries for correlation analysis, retrieve top-10 chunks with BM25, generate answers using eight LLMs, and compare Q-CARE with existing RAG metrics using correlation with human judgments; they also test conversational RAG and perform decomposition ablations.

key_findings.finding: Q-CARE produces fine-grained retrieval and generation measurements without requiring gold answers or gold evidence chunks, enabling the same framework to operate on both close-ended and open-ended queries.
Across the constructed benchmark, Q-CARE reports higher agreement with human judgments than the four compared RAG evaluation frameworks on the reported retrieval and generation dimensions.
The human-annotation study shows strong task-level agreement, with Fleiss' kappa between 0.801 and 0.891 for the three alignment tasks and over 97% agreement for decomposition verification.

Q-CARE's coverage and verifiability formulation transfers to conversational RAG, where it achieves the highest reported correlation on three of four datasets in both evaluated dimensions without changing the framework.
Query decomposition significantly improves Completeness across both close- and open-ended settings and both tested Qwen backbones, with reported gains from 0.056 to 0.473.
Decomposition does not uniformly improve every metric: for open-ended queries with the Qwen3-30B backbone, C-Prec@10 falls by 0.167 relative to the no-decomposition variant.
Using a stronger 80B evaluation backbone improves conversational correlation on six of eight dataset-dimension combinations, showing that evaluator quality remains dependent on the backbone model.

limitations: The evaluation pipeline still depends on strong LLMs for decomposition and alignment judgments, and results vary with evaluator backbone strength.
The principal human-correlation benchmark samples 160 close-ended and 160 open-ended queries, limiting the empirical coverage of the much larger space of possible RAG interactions.
The framework evaluates evidence coverage and verifiability but does not itself establish whether retrieved evidence is temporally current or drawn from the correct document version.
No calibrated abstention or selective-prediction risk guarantee is provided; the metrics diagnose quality rather than determine a statistically controlled stopping or refusal threshold.
The reported robustness studies span query types and conversational settings but do not directly test non-stationary temporal distribution shift.
Some experiments depend on proprietary API models, which can complicate exact long-term reproduction despite documented configurations and prompts.
raw_claims: Q-CARE is designed to evaluate RAG without gold answers or gold evidence chunks.
Queries are decomposed into sub-queries and generated answers into atomic claims.
C-Prec@k measures how much query-relevant information appears in retrieved chunks.
C-nDCG@k incorporates both sub-query coverage and retrieval rank.
Completeness measures the proportion of sub-queries addressed by the generated answer.
Conciseness measures how many answer claims are relevant to covered sub-queries.
Verifiableness measures how many answer claims can be checked against retrieved evidence.
The benchmark includes both close-ended and open-ended queries from eight datasets.
Human alignment labels show high inter-annotator agreement.
Q-CARE correlates more strongly with human judgments than the compared RAG metrics on the primary benchmark.
The framework can also be applied to conversational RAG evaluation.
Query decomposition materially improves completeness correlations in the ablation experiments.
Evaluator performance improves in several settings when the backbone is scaled from 30B to 80B.
The paper publicly releases its code and data.
